units.translation: But his flesh not even the hollow-bellied wolves will eat. where πάσονται [they will eat] is a correction in M, in which there is the gloss γεύσονται [they will taste].
about Clytaemnestra and Aegisthus: a lioness sleeping with a wolf.
For like a wolf, savage-minded.
But there is a saying that wolves are stronger than dogs.
so that double wolves carry a fawn.
Lycottas
one of the dogs of Actaeon, from Aeschylus (fr. 239) mentioned by Pollux 5, 47, where Bekker reads Λυκόττας [Lycottas] from the Paris manuscript. Commonly Λυκιτᾶς [Lycitas].

Lycitas
Lycurgus
was the title of a satyr play by Aeschylus (fr. 122-125), the fourth of the tetralogy which Aristophanes called Λυκούργειαν [the Lycurgeia] in Thesm. 136.
the Lycurgeia
ruin, harm
ruin, harm.
The usual meaning of the word is filth, dirt: see Thes. vol. 5 p. 431, but Aeschylus seems to have used it for λύμη [outrage, ruin], the word common in tragedy, which he uses at v. 147, 427.
sufferings hard to look upon, defilements, terrors.
outrage, ruin
to bring ruin upon, to harm
to bring ruin upon, to harm.
a body ruined by the bronze-wrought scale.
harming, destroying
harming, destroying.
he lies, the destroyer of this woman.
against the man, the destroyer of this house.
ruin, destruction
ruin, destruction.
with these adamant-bound outrages.
the Titan subdued by adamant-bound outrages.
for the ruin of the house.
by senseless outrage.
alas, alas, outrages: about which passage will be discussed under the word ὑλάσκω [to howl].
to cause pain, to grieve
to cause pain, to grieve. Passive λυποῦμαι [I am grieved] I grieve, I am distressed.
for whom it is possible neither to rejoice nor to grieve.
follow, and do not be grieved by the fire.
I am grieved
grief, sorrow
grief, sorrow.

the soul-destroying mind of grief, with clearly corrupt words, which the scholiast explains as ἥτις ἐστὶ θυμοβόρος λύπη τῆς φρενός [which is a soul-devouring grief of the mind]. What Aeschylus wrote is altogether uncertain: see what I said under the word θυμοφθόρος [soul-destroying].
and no bite of grief reaches my liver.
and grief without reward is your companion.
and without grief there is nowhere an overturning.
For what good is it to live a life that brings grief?
wretched, grievous
wretched, grievous.
wretched things, but joys for enemies.
going forward, do favors (thus partly Hermann, partly Schuetz for προπράσσων χάριτος [doing favors of grace]) of grievous anger, where Blomfield rightly reads λυγρᾶς [baneful].
and to me he is grievous, and he will not release him.
lyre
lyre.
without a lyre, nevertheless he sings.
Lyrnaeus
Lyrnaeus.

offspring Lyrnaeus, a handsome man. The scholiast noted nothing except ἀπὸ πόλεως [from the city]. Stephanus Byz. considered it the same as Λυρνησσός [Lyrnessus], which is a city of Mysia: Λυρνησσός [Lyrnessus]: a Trojan city, one of the eleven in the Troad. The ethnic is Λυρνήσσιος [Lyrnessian]; but Aeschylus in the Persians, as if from Λύρνα [Lyrna], has Λυρναῖος [Lyrnaeus]: but it is undoubtedly different.
